title: Inkling 2 Mini: Looped AI, Less Waiting
description:
Inkling 2 Mini, explained in 60 seconds: Thinking Machines' open-weights looped transformer (November 20, 2026) thinks more in its head, so you wait less.
An ordinary model writes its thinking out and you wait for every line; Inkling 2 Mini's middle 12 layers run 3 times with shared weights, so it writes less.

Read the maker's own announcement first: https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/

Chapters
0:00 Why you wait on AI
0:19 Same question, less waiting
0:36 Less writing, open weights
0:47 The honest catch

Status: released, open weights. Inkling 2 Mini came out on November 20, 2026 from Thinking Machines Lab under the Apache 2.0 license, on Hugging Face and Tinker.

The story: one hard exam question. You are the examiner with a stopwatch. An ordinary model (the standard non-looped transformer, where each token passes through the layers once) thinks harder by writing its working out, line after line, and you wait while it writes. Inkling 2 Mini works more of it over inside its head and hands in a shorter note, so there is less written thinking to wait through.

How it works: it is a 24-layer transformer. The middle 12 layers (layers 7 to 18, the two middle blocks of four blocks of six) run 3 times with shared weights, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights, with no new parameters. Thinking Machines says looping lets the model reason longer without writing its reasoning down, and reach the right answer with fewer tokens. In its test on a research variant (TML-d24-varloop-research), the mean reasoning tokens on GPQA Diamond fell from 3,703 at 1 pass to 1,731 at 3 passes, less than half. The weights are about 20 GB, which fits Apple silicon Macs with 32 GB or more memory.

The limits: it still writes some reasoning; even the minimum reasoning effort does not fully disable it. Each word it writes takes more work (the model card says compute per token is higher than the active-parameter count alone suggests), and speed varies by runtime and hardware, so this video gives no seconds figure: how much less you wait depends on your setup. The token numbers come from the research twin on one benchmark, not from the released model, which supports a fixed number of looping passes. Looping adds no knowledge: knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. The maker notes that reasoning not written down matters for monitoring, and reports that at this scale it sees no meaningful reduction in monitorability: the chain of thought grew shorter but stayed legible. The maker also says it is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat, and runtime support for looped models in local tools is new. This video makes no benchmark claim about Gemma 4 31B or Qwen3.8-27B; they appear only as examples of ordinary one-pass models in the maker's comparison table.

The takeaway: same exam; more of the working happens in its head.
